answers.solution:
We make our profession great by the way we do our work: with honesty, dedication, responsibility and, when needed, sacrifice. The passage says, "It is not the profession that makes us great; it is we that make our profession great."

Example: Anand Kumar's Super 30 programme has sent many underprivileged students to IITs, so the profession of teaching is seen as second to none. Similarly, Captain Vikram Batra and Captain Manoj Kumar Pandey laid down their lives for the country, which earned the highest respect for soldiers.
answers.finalAnswer: By doing our work with dedication, responsibility and sacrifice; e.g. Anand Kumar's Super 30 made teaching seem second to none

answers.solution: No, no profession can be considered the best. According to the passage, every profession is equally important, and calling one profession head and shoulders above others is preposterous. It is the nature of time and space (the situation we are in) that makes one profession seem more important: teachers matter most when we think of our children's education, doctors when we fall ill, and soldiers and the police when we think of the nation's security.
answers.finalAnswer: No; every profession is equally important, and only the time and situation make one seem more important

answers.solution: The passage advises young students to have big dreams and to pull out all the stops (make every possible effort) to achieve them. It also tells them that after achieving their dreams they must become responsible and productive citizens of their country; only then will they be assets of the society.
answers.finalAnswer: Have big dreams, work hard to achieve them, and become responsible and productive citizens

answers.solution: We make our profession look bad when we are careless or use our skills to do harm. For example, if a patient dies in a hospital because of a doctor's carelessness, society will not feel good about that profession. Similarly, if a scientist develops a deadly virus to destroy mankind, people of his profession may be seen as viruses by the world.
answers.finalAnswer: By carelessness or misuse of our work; e.g. a careless doctor letting a patient die

answers.solution:
(i) Ridiculous: preposterous ("...head and shoulders above others is definitely preposterous")
(ii) Wealth: assets ("...they cannot be considered assets of the society"; assets are valuable possessions, i.e. wealth)
(iii) Deprived: underprivileged ("...sent many underprivileged students to IITs")
answers.finalAnswer: preposterous; assets; underprivileged

answers.solution:
(i) To be a lot better than others: head and shoulders above (others)
(ii) Make a lot of effort: pull out all the stops
answers.finalAnswer: head and shoulders above; pull out all the stops

answers.solution: A suitable title is "The Road I Have Taken". The whole poem is about the road (path in life) the poet has chosen, its difficulties, and his decision to believe in it.
answers.finalAnswer: The Road I Have Taken

answers.solution: The poet feels hesitant to go ahead because the journey on the road he has chosen has been bumpy (full of difficulties), and the reality has turned out to be a little harsher than he expected.
answers.finalAnswer: Because the ride has been bumpy and the reality is harsher than expected

answers.solution: The poet will not blame his family because they meant well. They thought this was the road on which he would travel fastest, that is, succeed quickest.
answers.finalAnswer: Because they chose it thinking he would travel fastest on that road

answers.solution: The poet will not blame himself because he chose this road out of love: "No, I used to love it." Only the reality turned out to be a little harsher.
answers.finalAnswer: Because he used to love the road he chose

answers.solution: The poem tells us that every road (path in life) has its own difficulties; no life is a bed of roses. Other roads only look smoother and greener, but they have their own puddles. So we should not blame ourselves or others for the path we have chosen. Instead, we should believe that our road is the best, stay positive and always look forward to the best.
answers.finalAnswer: Every path in life has difficulties; believe your road is the best and keep looking forward

answers.solution:
1. Metaphor: the road stands for the path or career one chooses in life ("Each road is a life"), and "puddles" stand for problems and difficulties. "Not a bed of roses" also compares life to something that is not easy.
2. Rhetorical question: "Should I go ahead or not?" and "Should I blame myself for the road I have taken?" The poet asks questions to show his doubts, not to get answers from the reader.
(Repetition of "Should" and "road" is also used, to stress the poet's doubt and the idea of the journey.)
answers.finalAnswer: Metaphor (road = life; puddles = problems); rhetorical question (Should I go ahead or not?)

answers.solution:
(i) Bumpy: smoother ("Though appear smoother and greener")
(ii) Disbelief: believe ("Believe that your road is the best")
answers.finalAnswer: smoother; believe

Subject: How every resident can help make Delhi a healthier city

Sir/Madam,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to share how each resident of Delhi can help create a healthy environment in our city.

Delhi's air and water are becoming more polluted every year. The government alone cannot solve this problem; every citizen must play a part. Firstly, we should use public transport, share cars, or walk and cycle for short distances, so that fewer vehicles crowd the roads. Secondly, we must stop burning garbage and dry leaves, and separate wet and dry waste at home. Thirdly, every family can plant at least one tree and take care of it. We should also save water and electricity, avoid plastic bags and carry cloth bags instead. Resident welfare associations can organise cleanliness drives and awareness camps in their colonies.

If every resident adopts these small habits, Delhi can once again become a clean, green and healthy city for our children.

Yours faithfully,
Manisha

The Impact of ChatGPT on Education
by Arjun Rawat

ChatGPT, a computer program that can answer questions and write like a human, has entered our classrooms and homes. Its impact on education is both exciting and worrying.

On the positive side, ChatGPT works like a patient tutor available at any hour. A student who does not understand a lesson can ask it to explain the topic in simple words, give examples or check an answer. Teachers can use it to prepare worksheets, quizzes and lesson plans quickly. Students in villages, who may not have good tutors, can also get help easily.

However, there are dangers too. Some students copy their homework and essays from ChatGPT instead of thinking for themselves. This weakens their writing, reasoning and creativity. Moreover, ChatGPT sometimes gives wrong information with great confidence, so a student who trusts it blindly may learn mistakes.

ChatGPT is a tool, like a calculator. Used wisely, to understand and to practise, it can make learning faster and more enjoyable. Used to avoid effort, it can make students lazy. The choice lies with us.

(Topics chosen: (a) and (b))

(a) Child is the father of man.
This famous line by William Wordsworth means that the habits and qualities we form as children shape the kind of adult we become. A child who learns honesty, discipline and kindness grows into a responsible citizen, while a child who picks up bad habits often carries them into adult life. Therefore, parents and teachers must give children the right values early, and children themselves should build good habits, because today's child is tomorrow's man.

(b) One swallow does not make a summer.
The sight of a single swallow does not prove that summer has arrived. Similarly, one good result or one lucky event does not mean lasting success. A student who scores well in one test cannot assume he will top the final examination; he must keep working steadily. A team that wins one match is not yet the champion. This proverb teaches us not to become overconfident after a single success, but to be patient and consistent.

The Winning Goal

It was a bright Saturday afternoon, and the green ground near our colony was full of noise. Two junior football teams, the Blues and the Whites, were playing the final match of the summer league. Parents sat on folding chairs at the edge of the field, cheering loudly.

The score was 1-1 and only two minutes were left. Rohan, the smallest boy in the white team, had spent most of the match chasing the ball without touching it. Some boys had even laughed at him. Suddenly the ball rolled towards him. Kabir, the tallest player of the Blues, came running at him, and three other boys followed close behind.

Rohan did not panic. He remembered his coach's words: "Keep your eyes on the ball and your head down." He dodged Kabir, pushed the ball forward and kicked it with all his strength. The ball flew past the goalkeeper into the net!

The whistle blew. The Whites had won. His teammates lifted Rohan on their shoulders, and even Kabir came to shake his hand. That day everyone learned that size does not matter; courage and practice do.

My Favourite Video Game: Minecraft

Of all the video games I have played, my favourite is Minecraft, a game in which the whole world is made of blocks and the only limit is my imagination. When I start a new world, I find myself standing in an endless landscape of rolling green hills, thick forests, sparkling blue rivers and tall snow-capped mountains, all built from little square blocks. The sun rises slowly over the hills, sheep and cows wander lazily across the grass, and birds can be heard among the trees. I begin by punching a tree to collect wood, and from that simple start I craft tools: a wooden pickaxe, then a stone one, and finally a shining iron sword. As the sun sets and the sky turns orange and purple, I must hurry to build a shelter, because at night the world changes completely. Zombies groan in the darkness, skeletons rattle as they shoot arrows, and the green, hissing Creeper creeps silently towards me before exploding with a loud bang. My heart beats fast as I hide inside my small wooden hut, lit by flickering torches, waiting for morning. When day returns, the real adventure begins. I dig deep into dark caves where glowing lava bubbles and rare diamonds glitter on the walls. I build farms of golden wheat, tame wolves that follow me loyally, and construct huge castles with towers, bridges and secret rooms. Once I spent a whole week building a model of our school, with classrooms, a library and even a football ground, and I felt as proud as a real architect. I like Minecraft for many reasons. Firstly, it lets me be creative, because I can design and build anything I can dream of. Secondly, it teaches me to plan and solve problems: I must gather the right materials, manage my food and prepare for danger before night falls. Thirdly, it teaches patience, since big projects are built one block at a time. I also enjoy playing it with my cousins online, where we work as a team, share resources and build cities together, which has taught me cooperation. Unlike many games that are only about fighting, Minecraft rewards thinking and imagination. Of course, I play it only after finishing my studies and for a limited time, because too much screen time is harmful. Still, whenever I enter that world of blocks, I feel like an explorer, a builder and an adventurer all at once, and that is why Minecraft will always be my favourite video game.

(a) Though: conjunction (a subordinating conjunction joining the clause "he was angry" to the main clause).
(b) miserly: adjective (it describes the noun "person").
(c) Each: pronoun (a distributive pronoun; it stands alone in place of a noun, "each of you").
(d) Each: adjective (a distributive adjective; it comes before and qualifies the noun "boy").

answers.solution:
(a) I took breakfast two seconds ago.
Rule: a word of past time such as "ago" takes the simple past, not the present perfect.
(b) The Prime Minister leaves for London tomorrow.
Rule: a fixed, scheduled future plan is often written in the simple present ("The Prime Minister is leaving for London tomorrow" is also correct). Note: the sentence as printed, with "will leave", is already grammatically correct.
(c) He came to my house after I had had my lunch.
Rule: of two past actions, the one that happened first takes the past perfect.
(d) She came to my house while I was reading a novel.
Rule: an action in progress when another past action happened takes the past continuous.
answers.finalAnswer: I took breakfast two seconds ago.; The Prime Minister leaves for London tomorrow.; He came to my house after I had had my lunch.; She came to my house while I was reading a novel.
answers.notice: Sentence (b) is already correct as printed: 'will leave' is a correct way to speak of tomorrow. The simple present 'leaves' (or 'is leaving') is also correct for a fixed plan, and is the form the exercise most likely wanted.

(a) No other footballer in the world is as good as Lionel Messi.
(b) We do not know the girl's address. (The noun clause "where the girl lives" becomes a noun phrase.)
(c) He was poor, but he continued to have big dreams.
(d) Who does not admire Mahender Singh Dhoni?
(e) The soldier who was fearless was able to kill five terrorists single-handedly. (The adjective "fearless" becomes an adjective clause.)
(f) No sooner did we reach the stadium than the coach shouted at us.
(g) The meal was cooked by the chef.
(h) Raju said, "I completed the assignment yesterday." ("had completed" becomes "completed"; "the previous day" becomes "yesterday".)
(i) Why was the car not liked by your sister?
(j) Meena proposed to Tina that they should go to the theatre the next day. ("Let's" becomes "proposed/suggested that they should"; "tomorrow" becomes "the next day".)
answers.finalAnswer: No other footballer in the world is as good as Lionel Messi.; We do not know the girl's address.; He was poor, but he continued to have big dreams.; Who does not admire Mahender Singh Dhoni?; The soldier who was fearless was able to kill five terrorists single-handedly.; No sooner did we reach the stadium than the coach shouted at us.; The meal was cooked by the chef.; Raju said, "I completed the assignment yesterday."; Why was the car not liked by your sister?; Meena proposed to Tina that they should go to the theatre the next day.

answers.solution:
(a) To be excited or nervous: to have butterflies in one's stomach. (I had butterflies in my stomach before the interview.)
(b) Quickly or very fast: in a jiffy (also "like lightning"). (I will finish this work in a jiffy.)
(c) To avoid or shy away from danger: to steer clear of (danger). (Wise people steer clear of trouble.)
(d) To do something to get the attention of others: to play to the gallery (to show off). (The leader was only playing to the gallery.)
(e) Of a feeling being felt by everyone: in the air. (Excitement was in the air before the final match.)
answers.finalAnswer: to have butterflies in one's stomach; in a jiffy; to steer clear of (danger); to play to the gallery; in the air
answers.notice: More than one idiom fits some meanings: for (b) 'in a jiffy' and 'in the blink of an eye' are both right, and for (c) 'to steer clear of' and 'to fight shy of' are both right.

answers.solution:
(a) This: demonstrative adjective (determiner). It points out the noun 'car'.
(b) my: possessive adjective (possessive determiner). It shows whose car it is.
(c) left: past participle of the verb 'leave', used in the passive 'was left'.
(d) them: personal pronoun in the objective case, the object of the preposition 'by'.
(e) What: interrogative pronoun. It asks a question and stands for the thing asked about.
answers.finalAnswer: demonstrative adjective; possessive adjective; past participle (verb); personal pronoun (objective case); interrogative pronoun

answers.solution:
(a) Match
1. A game or contest: India won the cricket match.
2. A small stick used to light a fire: She lit the lamp with a match.

(b) Watch
1. A small clock worn on the wrist: My father gave me a new watch.
2. To look at carefully: We watch the news every evening.

(c) Ring
1. A round ornament worn on a finger: She wore a gold ring.
2. To make a bell sound: Please ring the bell when you arrive.

(d) Point
1. The sharp end of something: The point of this pencil is broken.
2. To show something with a finger: The child pointed at the aeroplane.

(e) Bear
1. A large wild animal with thick fur: We saw a bear in the zoo.
2. To tolerate or put up with: I cannot bear this noise any longer.
answers.finalAnswer: match: a game / a stick to light fire; watch: a timepiece / to look at; ring: an ornament for the finger / to sound a bell; point: a sharp end / to show with the finger; bear: an animal / to tolerate
